The General Fund statement carries a budget date of 12/13/22, reflecting a December budget amendment; the Food Service, Troy Career Center, Community Service, Troy Preschool, 2019 Capital Projects, Sinking and Capital Maintenance fund statements carry a budget date of 6/21/22. The funds reported are, in the order presented, the General Fund; the Consolidated Debt Service Funds; Special Revenue Fund - Food Service Fund (520); Special Revenue Fund - Troy Career Center Fund (529); Special Revenue Fund - Community Service Fund (530); Special Revenue Fund - Troy Preschool Fund (531); the 2019 Capital Projects Fund (419); the Sinking Fund (498); and the Capital Maintenance Fund (499), which appears in the original under the heading "Capital Maintence Fund." Each statement lists revenue by source, then expenditures by function or object, then total revenues, total expenditures, and a Revenues Over (Under) Expenditures line in both the budget and actual columns.

Expenditures: Salaries $644,719 / $258,339; Employee Benefits $326,134 / $116,121; Purchased Services $840,100 / $237,782; Supplies and Materials $34,000 / $42,556, the one line already past its annual budget; Other $110,000 with nothing spent; Outgoing Transfers $800,000 with nothing transferred. Expenditures: Salaries $1,155,601 / $447,233; Employee Benefits $602,878 / $203,029; Purchased Services $688,300 / $142,715; Supplies and Materials $124,000 / $54,425; Capital Outlay with no budget and $55,697 spent; Other $32,000 / $261; Debt Service $488,665 / $109,083; Outgoing Transfers $400,000 with nothing transferred. Total revenues $4,191,016 / $1,288,002; total expenditures $3,491,444 / $1,012,443; Revenues Over (Under) Expenditures $699,572 budgeted and $275,559 actual.

2019 CAPITAL PROJECTS FUND (419). Local Sources are budgeted at $10,000 with $88,519 received, far above the budgeted figure. Capital Outlay is budgeted at $8,756,222 with $3,960,004 spent. Total revenue $10,000 / $88,519; total expenditures $8,756,222 / $3,960,004; Revenues Over (Under) Expenditures $(8,746,222) budgeted and $(3,871,485) actual, as bond proceeds held from prior years are drawn down on construction.

SINKING FUND (498). Local Sources $4,442,000 budget / $2,199,484 actual; Capital Outlay $3,350,000 / $1,950,112. Total revenue $4,442,000 / $2,199,484; total expenditures $3,350,000 / $1,950,112; Revenues Over (Under) Expenditures $1,092,000 budgeted and $249,372 actual.

CAPITAL MAINTENANCE FUND (499). Local Sources and Incoming Transfers are both budgeted at zero with nothing received. Supplies are budgeted at $300,000 with nothing spent. Total revenue is zero in both columns; total expenditures $300,000 budgeted and nothing actual; Revenues Over (Under) Expenditures $(300,000) budgeted and zero actual.

Several lines across the report carry a budget with no corresponding activity: General Fund Transfers In and Other ($1,200,000), Consolidated Debt Service Principal ($15,965,000), Troy Career Center State Sources ($35,000) and Debt Service ($115,000), Community Service Federal Sources ($1,250,000), Other ($110,000) and Outgoing Transfers ($800,000), Troy Preschool Federal Sources ($450,000) and Outgoing Transfers ($400,000), and the entire Capital Maintenance Fund. Conversely, two lines show spending with no budget at all: Troy Preschool Capital Outlay at $55,697, and, on the revenue side, the 2019 Capital Projects Fund's Local Sources actual of $88,519 against a nominal $10,000 budget.

Taken together, the report shows a General Fund in which spending outpaced receipts for the period, chiefly because state aid and property tax revenue arrive unevenly across the year, while the Consolidated Debt Service Funds carried a large positive balance ahead of principal payments that had not yet come due. The two operating funds closest to break-even were the Food Service Fund, at $(5,028), and the Troy Career Center Fund, which matched revenue to expenditure exactly at $1,047,503.

2023_01_2023_ocsba_bylaw_amendments.paragraph: A four-item slate of proposed 2023 bylaw amendments for the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA), laid out in side-by-side "Currently Reads" and "Would Read" columns with a proposed change and rationale for each. The amendments touch Article VI (Election of Board of Directors), Article IX (Committees, two separate items in Section 4), and Article XI (Fiduciary and Financial Responsibilities). The most substantive change would let the OCSBA Board call a mid-year special election to increase the number of Directors, allowing seats to be restored twice per year rather than only once.
2023_01_2023_ocsba_bylaw_amendments.page:
**What it is**
The 2023 OCSBA Bylaw Amendments packet, distributed to member districts ahead of the Troy School District Board of Education meeting of February 14, 2023. Four amendments are presented in a two-column "Currently Reads" / "Would Read" format, each followed by a stated proposed change and rationale. New language is described as shown in blue.

**Amendment 1 - Article VI, Election of Board of Directors, Section 1: Number of Directors**
Existing text: the Board of Directors shall consist of an odd number of Directors, no fewer than 7 nor more than 9 members; the Board has discretion to set the number to best meet the needs of the Association; it shall consider a change whenever an election produces less candidates than open seats and prior to seeking candidates to fill a vacancy under Section 6; the Secretary shall promptly communicate any change to all Members; any decrease is accomplished by attrition, which may result in an eight member Board for up to one year until the next election; an increase is accomplished by election as outlined in Section 4.
Proposed change: add one sentence at the end - "In addition, the Board may call for a mid-year special election to increase the number of Directors."
Rationale: allows the Board to restore seats twice per year if necessary, rather than only once per year as in Section 4.

**Amendment 2 - Article IX, Committees, Section 4: Legislative Priorities**
Existing text: the Government Relations Committee will review/revise their Legislative Priorities annually, and revised Legislative Priorities will be submitted to the Board of Directors for approval by June 15th; once approved, they are provided to the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee and Member School Districts.
Proposed change: remove "by June 15th".
Rationale: the process needs to be moved up so that legislative priorities are adopted by the GRC in the fall (Sept/Oct), sent to the Board of Directors in October and then to Member Districts for voting, with consideration given to ending the voting period by the start of the common calendar's school break.

**Amendment 3 - Article IX, Committees, Section 4: Committee Membership/Leadership**
Existing text: committee members are appointed by the Board of Directors annually, may be reappointed for additional terms, and elect a Committee Chairperson at the first committee meeting after appointment.
Proposed change: add one sentence - "The Government Relations Committee Chairperson shall be a member of the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee."
Rationale: the Government Relations Committee (GRC) chair is not necessarily a member of the Board of Directors, and GRC Chair involvement is important to be sure the GRC's intent is reflected in resolutions.

**Amendment 4 - Article XI, Fiduciary and Financial Responsibilities, Section 2: Financial Reports**
Item (a) is unchanged: reports shall be completed on a timely basis and distributed to all Board members on a quarterly basis or upon request. Item (b) currently requires the Treasurer to present for approval by the Board of Directors an annual budget (July 1 to June 30) by June 30th along with an annual actual income and expense report by August 30th following the end of the fiscal year. It would be split into two numbered obligations: (1) no later than the June Board of Directors meeting, a budget for the upcoming fiscal year (July 1 to June 30); and (2) no later than August 30th, the end of year revenue and expense reports for the immediately preceding fiscal year.
Rationale: the current wording is confusing because the budget and the end of year reports are 2 separate documents.
2023_01_2023_ocsba_bylaw_amendments.verbose:
The 2023 OCSBA Bylaw Amendments packet sets out four proposed changes to the bylaws of the Oakland County School Boards Association, presented to the Troy School District Board of Education for the meeting of February 14, 2023. The document is formatted as a four-page comparison table, with each amendment shown twice - once under a "Currently Reads" heading and once under a "Would Read" heading - followed by a plain-language statement of the proposed change and the rationale behind it. New language is noted as being shown in blue in the original.

FIRST AMENDMENT: ARTICLE VI, ELECTION OF BOARD OF DIRECTORS, SECTION 1, NUMBER OF DIRECTORS. The existing section provides that the Board of Directors shall consist of an odd number of Directors, with no fewer than 7 nor more than 9 members, and that the Board of Directors shall have the discretion to determine the number of Directors to best meet the needs of the Association. The Board is directed to consider such a change whenever an election produces less candidates than open seats, and prior to seeking candidates to fill a vacancy under Section 6. The Secretary shall promptly communicate any change to the number of Directors to all Members. Any decrease in the number of Directors shall be accomplished by attrition, which may result in an eight member Board for up to one year, until the next election, while an increase in the number of Directors shall be accomplished by election, as outlined in Section 4. The proposed change adds a single sentence at the end of the section: "In addition, the Board may call for a mid-year special election to increase the number of Directors." The rationale given is that this allows the Board to restore seats twice per year if necessary, rather than only once per year as provided in Section 4.

SECOND AMENDMENT: ARTICLE IX, COMMITTEES, SECTION 4, LEGISLATIVE PRIORITIES. As currently written, the section states that the Government Relations Committee will review and revise their Legislative Priorities annually, that revised Legislative Priorities will be submitted to the Board of Directors for approval by June 15th, and that once approved by the Board, Legislative Priorities will be provided to the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee and Member School Districts. The proposed change is to remove the phrase "by June 15th," leaving the requirement that revised priorities be submitted to the Board of Directors for approval without a fixed deadline. The rationale states that the process needs to be moved up so that legislative priorities are adopted by the Government Relations Committee in the fall (September or October), sent to the Board of Directors in October, and then sent to Member Districts for voting, with the suggestion that the voting period end by the start of the common calendar's school break.

THIRD AMENDMENT: ARTICLE IX, COMMITTEES, SECTION 4, COMMITTEE MEMBERSHIP/LEADERSHIP. The current text provides that committee members will be appointed by the Board of Directors annually, that committee members may be reappointed for additional terms, and that the appointed committee members will elect a Committee Chairperson at the first committee meeting after appointment. The proposed change adds one sentence at the end of the paragraph: "The Government Relations Committee Chairperson shall be a member of the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee." The rationale explains that the Government Relations Committee (GRC) chair is not necessarily a member of the Board of Directors, and that GRC Chair involvement is important to be sure that the GRC's intent is reflected in resolutions.

FOURTH AMENDMENT: ARTICLE XI, FIDUCIARY AND FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITIES, SECTION 2, FINANCIAL REPORTS. The section opens with the requirement that the Treasurer shall maintain all financial statements, reports, and budgets, and this framing language is unchanged. Subsection (a) is also unchanged in both columns: reports shall be completed on a timely basis and distributed to all Board members on a quarterly basis or upon request. Subsection (b) currently requires that the Treasurer shall present for approval by the Board of Directors an annual budget covering July 1 to June 30 by June 30th, along with an annual actual income and expense report by August 30th following the end of the fiscal year. Under the proposed revision, subsection (b) would instead read that the Treasurer shall present for approval by the Board of Directors: (1) no later than the June Board of Directors meeting, a budget for the upcoming fiscal year (July 1 to June 30); and (2) no later than August 30th, the end of year revenue and expense reports for the immediately preceding fiscal year. The stated proposed change is to separate and clarify item (b), and the rationale is that the provision is confusing as written because the budget and the end of year reports are 2 separate documents.

Read together, the four amendments address governance flexibility in restoring vacant Director seats, the calendar for adopting and distributing OCSBA legislative priorities, the cross-membership of the Government Relations Committee Chairperson on the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee, and the drafting clarity of the Treasurer's reporting obligations. None of the amendments changes the permissible size range of the Board of Directors, which remains an odd number between 7 and 9 members, and none alters the quarterly financial reporting requirement in Article XI, Section 2(a).

2023_03_2023_ocsba_proposed_new_and_amen.paragraph: Oakland County School Boards Association resolutions material presented for the February 14, 2023 Troy Board of Education meeting, listing two proposed new 2023 resolutions, one proposed amendment to a previously adopted resolution, and the association's continuing resolutions with adoption dates and MASB cross-references. The new resolutions cover SCHOOL NUTRITION, backing expansion of the Free and Reduced Meals program to include all children as was done during the pandemic, and SCHOOL SAFETY, backing adequate state resources for schools. The proposed amendment concerns the School Finance Research Collaborative and insists that higher funded districts be held harmless while SFRC recommendations are implemented.
2023_03_2023_ocsba_proposed_new_and_amen.page:
**What it is**
The Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) resolutions packet circulated to member districts for the Troy School District Board of Education meeting of February 14, 2023. It sets out two proposed new resolutions, one proposed amendment to a previously adopted resolution, and the full list of continuing resolutions with their adoption and amendment dates and cross-references to Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) resolution numbers.

**Proposed new resolutions for 2023**
- SCHOOL NUTRITION: OCSBA supports the expansion of the Free and Reduced Meals program to include all children, as was done during the pandemic.
- SCHOOL SAFETY: OCSBA supports that there be adequate state resources to allow schools to both educate and keep students and staff safe.

2023_12_transmittal_letter_for_fy24_prop.page:
**What it is**
Transmittal letter dated March 21, 2023 from Dr. Wanda Cook-Robinson, Superintendent of Oakland Schools, addressed "Dear Board of Education Designate," accompanying the proposed FY 2023-24 Oakland Schools budget documents. Copies went to the District Superintendent and District Business Manager.

**Statutory process**
Under Michigan School Code Section 380.624(2) the proposed FY 2023-24 General Fund budget is submitted to constituent districts' Boards of Education for review by May 1. Not later than June 1, the board of each constituent district shall adopt a resolution of support or non-support of the General Fund budget. Budgets for all Oakland Schools funds are included for transparency, but constituent districts vote only on the General Fund budget.

**Revenue outlook**
Oakland Schools is primarily funded by property tax dollars, with a projected growth factor in property tax revenues of 5.0%. Projections are described as conservative compared to Oakland County taxable value increase projections because actual taxable value figures are not available during budget preparation. For the first time in eight years, a Headlee rollback is not being budgeted; additional information on taxable values and the millage reduction factor will be received by June 1.

**Major budget features**
- Mental health: two mental health consultants were added in 2022-23, with the work continuing in 2023-24 under Section 31n of the Revised School Aid Act; programs include PREPaRE, Behavioral Threat Assessment and Management (BTAM), Suicide Assessment, Life Space Crisis Intervention and Non-Violent Crisis Intervention, with a county-wide summit the first week in August.
- School safety: funding for four school resource officers from the Oakland County Sheriff's Department, with 50% of one SRO funded by a Michigan State Police grant and the rest through the Career and Technical Education millage; approximately $8 million for safety and security updates at the four technical campuses.
- Cybersecurity: multi-factor authentication, an endpoint detection and response platform for local districts, and phishing simulation exercises.
- Shared services: technology services to sixteen constituent districts; business office services on a limited basis to five districts through an intergovernmental agreement.
- MiPEER: formed in FY 2012-13 by Oakland Schools and 22 Oakland County school districts, using BusinessPLUS; a new Time and Attendance solution arrives in 2023-24.
- LEO 2.0: a $5 million research-based literacy initiative, originally launched in 2019-20.
- Subsidies: over $1.3 million for software and instructional tools in CTE and curriculum and assessment.
- Countywide communications channel: $700,000 for an emergency radio channel linking districts to first responders.

**Personnel and benefits**

| Item | Figure |
| --- | --- |
| Nonunion salary increase | 2.5% |
| Union salary increase | 1% |
| Basic/MIP with Health Care Premium Subsidy retirement rate beginning October 1, 2023 | 31.34% |
| Projected blended retirement rate 2023-24 | 30.2% |
| Projected Medical CPI growth | 3.7% |

Hard cap health care limits: Family $20,180.43 for plan years beginning after 1/1/23 and a projected $20,927.11 after 1/1/24; Individual plus one $15,474.60 and $16,047.16; Single $7,399.47 and $7,673.25.

**PA-18 special education**
The base distribution of PA-18 funding to local school districts is budgeted to increase approximately $11.0 million or 7.4%, with $2.5 million budgeted for other LEA distributions covering group home expenditures, reimbursements for educating incarcerated youth, special education program startup, extraordinary expenditures and capital. In FY 2022-23 Oakland Schools distributed additional PA-18 funds totaling $3.7 million above the base distribution.

**Calendar**

2023_12_transmittal_letter_for_fy24_prop.verbose:
Dated March 21, 2023 and opening "Dear Board of Education Designate," this is the transmittal letter from Dr. Wanda Cook-Robinson, Superintendent of Oakland Schools, that accompanies the proposed FY 2023-24 Oakland Schools budget documents sent to constituent districts, including Troy School District, and placed before the Troy Board of Education on May 16, 2023. Copies are directed to the District Superintendent and the District Business Manager.

STATUTORY FRAMEWORK. Per the Michigan School Code, Section 380.624(2), the proposed FY 2023-24 General Fund budget is to be submitted to its constituent districts' Boards of Education for review by May 1. Not later than June 1, the board of each constituent district shall adopt a resolution of support or non-support of the General Fund budget. For transparency purposes Oakland Schools includes the budgets for all of its funds in the enclosed document, but it is only the General Fund budget upon which constituent districts vote, and LEA Designates are only voting on the General Fund budget.

PROPERTY TAX AND HEADLEE. Oakland Schools is primarily funded by property tax dollars, and the letter states a projected growth factor in Oakland Schools' property tax revenues of 5.0%. Tax revenue projections are described as conservative compared to Oakland County taxable value increase projections, since actual taxable value figures are not available during preparation of the budget. For the first time in eight years, a Headlee rollback is not being budgeted. The letter explains that a Headlee rollback occurs when the annual growth on existing property is greater than the rate of inflation as measured by the Consumer Price Index, and notes that additional information will be received by June 1 regarding taxable values and the millage reduction factor.

SOCIAL-EMOTIONAL WELLBEING AND MENTAL HEALTH SUPPORT. Oakland Schools shifted resources toward mental health support by adding two mental health consultants in 2022-23 and continues that work in 2023-24, broadening the support of mental health workers in schools under Section 31n of the Revised School Aid Act. The mental health team is responsible for oversight and provision of intensive mental health and complex behavior support, and for school-wide school safety and crisis preparedness and response initiatives, specifically naming PREPaRE, Behavioral Threat Assessment and Management (BTAM), Suicide Assessment, Life Space Crisis Intervention, and Non-Violent Crisis Intervention. Professional Learning events focused on engaging stakeholders in ensuring supports that address the wellbeing needs of the whole child are scheduled throughout the 2023-24 year, beginning with a county-wide summit the first week in August.

SCHOOL SAFETY. The 2023-24 budget contains funding for four school resource officers (SROs) to be provided by the Oakland County Sheriff's Department. Funding for 50% of one SRO is provided through a grant by the Michigan State Police, while the remaining officers are funded through the Career and Technical Education millage. The District is also planning safety and security updates at the four technical campuses, with approximately $8 million provided in the 2023-24 budget for these projects.

CYBERSECURITY. To maintain the safety, security and integrity of applications and data managed by Oakland Schools, significant investments are being made in cybersecurity, including increasing the use of multi-factor authentication, implementing an endpoint detection and response platform for local districts to detect and thwart security threats, and conducting cybersecurity awareness and phishing simulation exercises. Significant supports are available to constituent districts to assist with cybersecurity awareness and evaluation.

SHARED SERVICES. Oakland Schools provides technology, business office, instruction and truancy services on a cost-recovery basis. Technology services are currently being provided to sixteen constituent districts, and business office services are currently being provided on a limited basis to five districts through an intergovernmental agreement (IGA) with Oakland Schools.

MiPEER CONSORTIUM. In FY 2012-13, Oakland Schools and 22 Oakland County school districts formed the Michigan Partnership for Essential Education Resources (MIPEER) to select a countywide Enterprise Resource Planning system for human resource and financial applications. Since then the Consortium has standardized the Chart of Accounts for the selected solution, BusinessPLUS, and created best practice business processes for finance, human resources, budgeting and procurement. In 2023-24, Consortium members will be able to participate in a new Time and Attendance solution that will integrate with the existing BusinessPLUS product.

LITERACY ESSENTIALS OAKLAND (LEO) 2.0. The LEO project, initially kicked off in 2019-20, has been reimagined and relaunched as LEO 2.0, a $5 million research-based literacy initiative tailored to the needs of local districts, building capacity and focused on job-embedded professional learning. During 2023-24 the LEO 2.0 team will continue working with the countywide coaching network and district Literacy Leadership Teams on building capacity for early literacy success.

SUBSIDIES. Oakland Schools provides over $1.3 million in subsidies for software and other instructional tools in the areas of Career and Technical Education and curriculum and assessment. The subsidies in the 2023-24 budget are detailed within the budget document and are exclusive of pass-through grant funds, other district allocations, and the cost of dedicated staff who support student and finance/HR software and applications.

COUNTYWIDE COMMUNICATIONS CHANNEL. The 2023-24 General Education Fund budget includes costs for a countywide communications channel in the amount of $700,000, intended to connect constituent districts to first responders via an emergency radio channel.

PERSONNEL COSTS. Step increases for eligible employees are included in the 2023-24 budget along with a 2.5% salary increase for nonunion staff and a 1% increase for union staff. All union salary changes including step adjustments are subject to collective bargaining, and the increase cited is in accordance with the current bargaining agreement. On the State-mandated retirement rate, there are 8 rates in effect depending on the hire date of employees and their choices for eventual retirement benefits; the most common employee choice is Basic/MIP with Health Care Premium Subsidy, whose rate is projected to increase to 31.34% beginning October 1, 2023. Oakland Schools analyzed its own employee choices and projected an overall blended retirement rate of 30.2% for 2023-24.

HEALTH CARE HARD CAP. The "Hard Cap" for employee health care costs remains in effect for all labor groups. The dollar limits employers may pay are subject to annual adjustment based on the medical price index, over which the school district has no jurisdiction. Oakland Schools has projected growth in the medical price index of 3.7%. For plan years beginning after 1/1/23 and, on the projected basis, after 1/1/24, the limits are: Family $20,180.43 rising to $20,927.11; Individual plus one $15,474.60 rising to $16,047.16; and Single $7,399.47 rising to $7,673.25.

PA-18 SPECIAL EDUCATION FUNDING. Oakland Schools receives property tax revenue for support of Special Education programs. The base distribution of PA-18 funding to local school districts is budgeted to increase approximately $11.0 million or 7.4%. Additionally, $2.5 million is budgeted for other LEA distributions covering group home expenditures, reimbursements to districts for educating incarcerated youth, special education program startup and extraordinary expenditures, and capital. In FY 2022-23, Oakland Schools distributed additional PA-18 funds totaling $3.7 million above the base distribution.

PLANNING FOR THE FUTURE. Oakland Schools uses a five-year forecast updated with each budget amendment that incorporates projections from Oakland County Equalization for taxable values, and maintains a five-year capital plan updated annually. The organization pre-funds at least three years and up to five years of the capital plan requirements.

CALENDAR AND CONTACT. A presentation of the budget to the 28 local school district business managers was scheduled to occur at their meeting of the Oakland County School Business Officials on April 14, 2023. The Oakland Schools Board of Education would then hold a Designates Meeting on April 20 at 6:00 PM, giving local board designates and district administration an opportunity to review the General Fund budget before submitting their board's resolution to Oakland Schools on or before June 1, 2023. The Oakland Schools Board of Education will hold a Truth in Budgeting hearing on June 6 and will consider the FY 2023-24 proposed budget documents for approval during its regular meeting that night. Questions may be directed to the Superintendent's office at 248.209.2424.
